intro: Variation III of Elgar’s “Enigma” Variations, Op. 36, “R.B.T.” (Allegretto), portrays Richard Baxter Townshend, who played an old man in amateur theatricals, his bass voice suddenly shooting up into a squeak. Elgar gave the scene to the oboe and bassoons.

sections.label: Var 3 · Allegretto, oboe and bassoons
sections.mNote: An oboe melody over bassoons in the low register.

cues.title: Oboe solo with bassoons
cues.text: The solo oboe plays a varied form of the theme, marked scherzando. Bassoons reply below it over pizzicato strings.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, p. 15, rehearsal 8: solo oboe marked scherzando, bassoon replies and pizzicato strings. Elgar describes the oboe’s pert theme and the bassoons’ growing grumpiness in his commentary on variation III: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Richard Baxter Townshend
cues.text: Townshend was an Oxford don and the author of the Tenderfoot books. Elgar recalled his amateur acting in the part of an old man whose low voice kept flying into soprano. His brother-in-law, William Meath Baker, is the subject of the next variation.
cues.evidence: Townshend’s occupation, books, family relationship and Elgar’s recollection of the performance: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations, variation III, citing Elgar, My Friends Pictured Within (Novello, 1946).

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: Novello full score, pp. 15–19, rehearsal figures 8–10, with first and second endings on p. 19: oboe, bassoon and string exchanges.

timeline.note: Oboe and bassoons trade phrases above plucked strings, with contrabassoon joining the low replies (p. 15).
Horns and timpani join the wind and string exchanges (pp. 16–17).
Bassoons and clarinets take up short phrases over the quieter strings (p. 18).
The repeat brings back the violin melody and its accented wind replies (pp. 16–19).
Short wind phrases and fading strings close the variation, with horns and timpani in the cadence (p. 19).

composer.epithet: Composer of the Enigma Variations, a set of variations drawn from his friendships, who also recorded his own music for the gramophone.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn as a member of the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. He knew each player in this orchestra individually and had to write within their capabilities. He also taught in local schools and gave private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
